claims.text: The starting material is a superconducting, single-phase, disordered solid solution containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
Local short-range chemical order is the primary factor governing superconductivity in the proposed high-entropy alloy.
Short-range chemical order tunes superconducting transition temperature by modulating electron-phonon coupling strength.
Rapid quenching preserves a greater degree of chemical disorder.
Minor compositional adjustments can favor clustering of heavy transition metals.
Changes in the local elemental distribution alter lattice vibrational modes.
Altered lattice vibrational modes change electron-phonon coupling strength.
Enhanced short-range order can cause phonon softening.
Phonon softening increases effective electron-phonon coupling.
Increased electron-phonon coupling raises the superconducting transition temperature.
Greater chemical disorder lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
Annealed samples with enhanced local order will have a higher transition temperature than the as-cast baseline.
Annealed samples will show stronger electron-phonon coupling signatures than the as-cast baseline.
Rapidly quenched samples will have a lower transition temperature than the as-cast baseline.
The proposed relationship applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution and every constituent remains at or above 5 at.%.
Phase separation or competing electronic correlations may invalidate the proposed relationship between local order and superconductivity.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits minor compositional adjustments, whereas the conditions require identical overall stoichiometry and the falsification experiment specifies the same alloy composition. A composition-adjustment arm would therefore violate the stated controlled-comparison condition.
